Martina Navratilova. A Czech-American tennis icon who won eighteen Grand Slam singles titles and became one of the sport's greatest players with an aggressive serve-and-volley game and unmatched athleticism. Her seven Wimbledon titles and fifty-nine major titles across singles, doubles, and mixed doubles set standards of dominance unmatched in women's tennis history. She won three Australian Opens, four French Opens, seven Wimbledons, and four US Opens between 1983 and 1984, and again in 1986 and 1987. She won fifty-nine Grand Slam titles across all categories—singles, doubles, and mixed doubles—the highest total by any player in history. Her dominance in doubles rivaled her singles record, making her a force across multiple competitions. She defected from Czechoslovakia to the United States in 1975, becoming a pioneering advocate for LGBTQ plus rights in sports. Her openness about her identity was groundbreaking for the era and helped transform discussions in professional athletics. Known for her serve-and-volley game, exceptional athleticism, and her fierce rivalry with Chris Evert across a sixteen-year span, she was a transformative player who redefined women's tennis. She reached world number one in 1978 and held it for a then-record 186 weeks, dominating the late 1970s and 1980s. She continued competing at high levels into her forties, her longevity unprecedented for women's tennis at that time and an inspiration to younger players.
